column1: For outer Product AS p, correlate inner Product AS p2 with WHERE p2.CategoryID = {{c1::p.CategoryID}}.
column2:
Use the outer alias to make the dependency explicit. The average or lookup then uses the current product's category.
Review source

column1: With non-NULL CategoryIDs and outer Product AS p, (SELECT {{c1::AVG}}(p2.Price) FROM Product AS p2 WHERE p2.CategoryID = p.CategoryID) computes its category mean.
column2:
The WHERE clause defines the category before AVG calculates the mean. AVG ignores NULL prices.
Review source

column1: A SELECT-list scalar subquery must project exactly {{c1::one column}}.
column2:
The expression must also return at most one row. Zero matching rows yield SQL NULL.
Review source

column1: For each customer, a correlated {{c1::MAX}}(o.OrderDate) returns the latest matching order date.
column2:
The aggregate finds the most recent date for one customer at a time. With no matches its result is NULL.
Review source

column1: To count every matching order, a SELECT-list correlated aggregate can use {{c1::COUNT(*)}} without GROUP BY.
column2:
COUNT(*) includes matching rows even if an individual column is NULL. With no matches the ungrouped count produces zero.
Review source

column1: With non-NULL CategoryIDs and outer Product AS p, filter above its category mean with p.Price {{c1::>}} (SELECT AVG(p2.Price) FROM Product AS p2 WHERE p2.CategoryID = p.CategoryID).
column2:
This uses a strict comparison so a price equal to the category mean does not qualify.
Review source

column1: For outer Customer AS c, keep customers with orders using WHERE {{c1::EXISTS}} (SELECT 1 FROM Orders AS o WHERE o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID).
column2:
EXISTS keeps a customer once regardless of how many matching orders the inner query finds.
Review source

column1: For outer Customer AS c, keep customers without orders using WHERE {{c1::NOT EXISTS}} (SELECT 1 FROM Orders AS o WHERE o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID).
column2:
NOT EXISTS is true when the matching set is empty. It does not compare the values in the inner SELECT list.
Review source

column1: The SQL predicate EXISTS (SELECT NULL) evaluates to {{c1::TRUE}}.
column2:
The scalar value is NULL but there is still one row. EXISTS tests row presence only.
Review source

column1: To exclude empty categories from a no-violations rule, also require a correlated {{c1::EXISTS}} over their products.
column2:
The second predicate requires a product to exist. The no-violations predicate separately rejects any disallowed prices.
Review source

column1: Treat missing prices as violations with (p.Price <= 100 {{c1::OR p.Price IS NULL}}).
column2:
The explicit test includes missing prices in the set of violations. Without it, a comparison with NULL yields UNKNOWN.
Review source

column1: For outer Product AS p, test top-three ID membership with WHERE p.ProductID {{c1::IN}} (SELECT TOP (3) p2.ProductID FROM Product AS p2 WHERE p2.CategoryID = p.CategoryID ORDER BY p2.Price DESC).
column2:
The IN predicate checks the current product's ID against the selected category IDs. Add a tie rule if tied prices affect which IDs are selected.
Review source

column1: With unique ProductID, ORDER BY Price DESC, {{c1::ProductID ASC}} makes TOP selection repeatable with lower IDs first among price ties.
column2:
The second key defines which equal-priced product comes first. The complete sort order has no ties when IDs are unique.
Review source

column1: For price-only ordering, TOP (3) {{c1::WITH TIES}} includes all ties at the cutoff price.
column2:
If several products share the third row's price, they all qualify. The result can contain more than three rows.
Review source

column1: For non-NULL categories and prices, top-three-with-ties filtering compares the correlated count of strictly higher-priced rows {{c1::<}} 3.
column2:
Fewer than three rows priced higher means the product falls within the first three positions or ties at the cutoff.
Review source

column1: Among earlier orders of the same customer, TOP (1) ORDER BY OrderDate {{c1::DESC}} picks the latest earlier date.
column2:
Descending order visits the most recent qualifying timestamp first. It does not resolve ties on that timestamp by itself.
Review source

column1: For ascending (OrderDate, unique OrderID), an equal-date predecessor of o satisfies o2.OrderID {{c1::<}} o.OrderID.
column2:
The ID comparison defines which tied timestamps precede the current order. Reverse both keys in the lookup to get the closest one.
Review source

column1: A SELECT-list TOP (1) previous-order subquery with no qualifying row yields {{c1::NULL}}.
column2:
An empty lookup contributes SQL NULL to the outer row. Use a replacement value explicitly only when it has the desired meaning.
Review source

column1: (SELECT MAX(o.OrderDate) FROM Orders AS o WHERE o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID) returns {{c1::NULL}} when no orders match outer customer c.
column2:
MAX over no matching orders has a NULL result. The aggregate still returns one row, unlike an empty TOP lookup.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server, report query reads with SET STATISTICS {{c1::IO}} ON;
column2:
Compare logical reads for representative inputs. Fewer reads can help explain a faster query but do not alone prove lower elapsed time.
Review source
